oil.summary: Crude markets staged a dramatic intraday divergence on Tuesday. WTI cratered 4.74% to $91.23/bbl while Brent held relatively firm, slipping only 0.39% to just under $100. The catalyst was Saudi Arabia's restart of the East-West pipeline — a 4 mb/d route that had been the kingdom's primary export artery — easing the most acute supply-disruption fears. Separately, Aramco signalled to Asian refiners that Yanbu cargoes would soon resume. However, ING cautioned that supply-side risks remain elevated, with VLCC freight costs exploding as Gulf risk keeps tankers trapped. The Russia sanctions complex adds further noise: Trump signed secondary sanctions threatening India and China with 100% tariffs on Russian oil purchases, prompting Indian refiners to weigh import cuts, even as a separate temporary US easing of Russia sanctions was reported to cap prices. RBOB gasoline bore the sharpest selling, down 6.70%.
drivers: Saudi East-West pipeline restart and Yanbu port reopening signal sharply reduced near-term supply disruption, triggering aggressive WTI sell-off
New US secondary sanctions (100% tariff threat) on buyers of Russian oil — including India and China — reshaping global crude trade flows
Persistent market tightness flagged by ING: VLCC freight costs surging and Strait of Hormuz risk ongoing amid US-Iran conflict

gas.summary: Henry Hub surged 9.87% on the day to $3.116/MMBtu, extending a strong one-month rally of over 12%, likely reflecting spillover risk appetite from the broader Middle East supply crunch and tightening LNG balances. European TTF was far more subdued, adding just 0.85% to €73.875/MWh on the day, though it remains up 12% on the month. The industrial demand destruction story is already playing out: INEOS announced it is idling three UK chemical plants, citing uncompetitive European gas prices. A new armed-group blockade at Libya's Sharara oilfield — the country's largest — threatens associated gas production and adds incremental upside risk. A headline noting soaring oil and gas prices will push eurozone inflation above target into 2027 underscores the macro stakes.
drivers: Henry Hub +9.87% on the day, likely driven by LNG export demand tightness and Middle East risk contagion
European industrial demand destruction accelerating: INEOS idling three UK plants on uncompetitive gas costs
Libya's Sharara oilfield blockade by armed group adds fresh supply risk to gas-linked production

power.summary: EU Carbon EUAs were essentially flat at $82.505/EUA (-0.04% on the day), consolidating after a 5.67% monthly gain. With TTF up 12% on the month, power generation costs remain elevated, and a market commentary published today warned that rising utility fuel costs, capital costs, and raw materials are combining to push electricity prices higher — with utility profit margins potentially becoming a political target. Europe's offshore wind sector offered no near-term relief: a headline flagged that the monopile manufacturing market has swung from capacity shortage to weak utilization, signalling a slowdown in new build. Geopolitical macro noise — Yemen escalation, expanded US Iran sanctions including potential grounding of Iranian airlines — keeps broader energy risk premiums supported, indirectly underpinning carbon prices. Data flow for this sector today was relatively thin.
drivers: EUAs flat near $82.50 but monthly trend firm (+5.67%), supported by elevated TTF and persistent energy inflation
Utility sector facing a cost squeeze from fuel, capital, and raw materials simultaneously, with political scrutiny of profit margins flagged
Europe's offshore wind build-out slowing — weak monopile factory utilization signals near-term renewable capacity addition disappointment
